h1: What Can a 5 kVA Generator Run?
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: kva
fields.label: Generator size
fields.hint: The kVA on the generator's nameplate. If the label gives kW, the kW figure is already the usable watts.

fields.hint: Running load × this margin must fit the capacity, so the engine is not run flat out for hours.

answer: A {{out.kva|1}} kVA generator gives {{out.capacity_w|int}} W at {{out.pf|2}} power factor: about {{out.max_running_w|int}} W of continuous running load and {{out.max_start_w|int}} W for the moment a motor starts. That runs {{out.appliance_count|int}} inverter ACs of 1.5 ton on their own, or one 1.5 ton inverter AC with fans, lights, a fridge and a TV ({{out.running_w|int}} W). Usable watts = kVA × 1,000 × power factor.
how: {{out.kva|1}} kVA × 1,000 × {{out.pf|2}} power factor = {{out.capacity_w|int}} W. Running load may use {{out.capacity_w|int}} W ÷ {{out.margin|2}} margin = {{out.max_running_w|int}} W; a starting surge may reach the full {{out.max_start_w|int}} W. Your list runs at {{out.running_w|int}} W ({{out.load_pct|int}}% of the running capacity, {{out.spare_running_w|int}} W spare) and peaks at {{out.peak_w|int}} W when its largest motor starts. The {{out.appliance_name|raw}} runs at {{out.appliance_run_w|int}} W and starts at {{out.appliance_start_w|int}} W, so this generator runs {{out.appliance_count|int}} of them: all running and one starting must both fit.
key_facts: A generator's usable power in watts = nameplate kVA × 1,000 × power factor; at the usual {{d.pf_generator|2}} a {{d.standard_generator_kva.3|1}} kVA set gives {{out.capacity_w|int}} W, a {{d.standard_generator_kva.1|1}} kVA set {{ex.1.out.capacity_w|int}} W and a {{d.standard_generator_kva.5|1}} kVA set {{ex.3.out.capacity_w|int}} W.
Two limits apply at once: the running load times a {{d.margin|2}} margin must fit the capacity, and the running load plus the largest starting surge must not exceed the capacity even for a second.

A {{d.standard_generator_kva.3|1}} kVA generator runs a 1.5 ton inverter AC ({{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.running_w|int}} W running, {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.starting_w|int}} W maximum) with fans, lights and a fridge, but it cannot start a 1.5 ton non-inverter AC whose compressor needs about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W for a moment, more than its {{out.capacity_w|int}} W.

A {{d.standard_generator_kva.1|1}} kVA generator carries about {{ex.1.out.max_running_w|int}} W of running load: fans, lights, a TV and a non-inverter fridge, whose {{a.refrigerator-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W start fits inside its {{ex.1.out.capacity_w|int}} W.

formula.text: P_cap = kVA × 1000 × PF; fits if P_run × margin ≤ P_cap and P_run + max(P_start − P_run) ≤ P_cap; n = floor(min(P_cap ÷ (P_run × margin), (P_cap − P_start) ÷ P_run + 1))
lines: P_cap = generator capacity in watts, PF = power factor (nameplate convention 0.8)
P_run = running watts of everything on at once; margin = continuous load margin
P_start = starting watts of the largest motor or compressor (only one starts at a time)
n = how many of one appliance the generator runs, all running and one of them starting
This is the generator sizing rule solved for the load, so it never contradicts the generator size pages

sections.h2: What can a 5 kVA generator run at the same time?
p: A {{out.kva|1}} kVA generator has {{out.capacity_w|int}} W to give. Keep the steady load under {{out.max_running_w|int}} W so the engine is not working flat out, and keep the moment of the largest motor start under {{out.max_start_w|int}} W. The default list, four fans, ten LED bulbs, an inverter fridge, a TV and a 1.5 ton inverter AC, runs at {{out.running_w|int}} W and peaks at {{out.peak_w|int}} W, so it fits with {{out.spare_running_w|int}} W of running load to spare.

That spare room is enough for an iron or a microwave for a few minutes, but not for a second inverter AC with everything else on. On its own the generator runs {{out.appliance_count|int}} inverter ACs of 1.5 ton; with the fans, fridge and lights running as well, one is the practical limit. Edit the list above to test your own home.

sections.h2: 5 kVA generator load capacity and the non-inverter AC
p: By the sizing rule used across this site, a {{d.standard_generator_kva.3|1}} kVA generator cannot start a 1.5 ton non-inverter AC. The AC runs at only {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-non-inverter.running_w|int}} W, well within the running limit, but its compressor is a plain motor that draws about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W for a second or two while it starts. That is more than the {{out.capacity_w|int}} W the generator can supply, so the voltage dips, the AC may trip on low voltage or the generator's breaker opens. The counter for that AC above shows {{ex.2.out.appliance_count|int}} on a {{ex.2.out.kva|1}} kVA set.

At {{ex.3.out.kva|1}} kVA ({{ex.3.out.capacity_w|int}} W) the same AC starts with fans and lights, peaking at {{ex.3.out.peak_w|int}} W. With a non-inverter fridge also running, the start peak is {{ex.2.out.peak_w|int}} W, which is more than {{ex.3.out.capacity_w|int}} W, so the generator size for a 1.5 ton AC page, which sizes the set for the AC plus the rest of the house, lands on a larger set. Some owners do start a non-inverter AC on a smaller generator because the real surge of their unit is lower or shorter than the planning figure; the calculator does not promise that, and a soft starter or an inverter AC is the safer fix.

sections.h2: What can a 3 kVA generator run?
p: A {{ex.1.out.kva|1}} kVA generator gives {{ex.1.out.capacity_w|int}} W, about {{ex.1.out.max_running_w|int}} W of steady load. That covers the basics during loadshedding: four fans, ten LED bulbs, a TV and a non-inverter fridge come to {{ex.1.out.running_w|int}} W, and the fridge's {{a.refrigerator-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W start takes the peak to {{ex.1.out.peak_w|int}} W, still inside the capacity. On its own it could run {{ex.1.out.appliance_count|int}} such fridges.

A 3 kVA set can run a 1 ton inverter AC on its own ({{a.ac-split-1ton-inverter.running_w|int}} W running, {{a.ac-split-1ton-inverter.starting_w|int}} W maximum), but not together with a non-inverter fridge and a full set of fans; the list above lets you check the exact mix. A 1.5 ton inverter AC fits only with very little else running.

sections.h2: Can a 2.5 kVA generator run an AC?
p: A {{ex.0.out.kva|1}} kVA generator gives {{ex.0.out.capacity_w|int}} W, with {{ex.0.out.max_running_w|int}} W for steady running. A 1 ton inverter AC with two fans and six LED bulbs runs at {{ex.0.out.running_w|int}} W, {{ex.0.out.load_pct|int}}% of the running capacity, and peaks at {{ex.0.out.peak_w|int}} W, so that combination works. Any non-inverter AC is out: even the 1 ton size starts at about {{a.ac-split-1ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W.
Many 2.5 kVA sets are sold as 2 kW units, which is the same thing: kW is the usable watts after the power factor. Check which figure is on your nameplate before you compare.

sections.h2: 7 kVA and 10 kVA generator capacity for a whole home
p: At {{ex.3.out.kva|1}} kVA ({{ex.3.out.capacity_w|int}} W) a generator can start one 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with fans and lights: the list runs at {{ex.3.out.running_w|int}} W and peaks at {{ex.3.out.peak_w|int}} W. Add a running non-inverter fridge and the start peak of {{ex.2.out.peak_w|int}} W is above the capacity, so either stagger the starts or choose {{ex.4.out.kva|1}} kVA. Two non-inverter ACs do not fit until the second one's start is covered on top of the first one running.

At {{ex.4.out.kva|1}} kVA ({{ex.4.out.capacity_w|int}} W, {{ex.4.out.max_running_w|int}} W steady) two 1.5 ton inverter ACs, six fans, twelve bulbs, an inverter fridge and a 1 hp water pump run together at {{ex.4.out.running_w|int}} W, peaking at {{ex.4.out.peak_w|int}} W when the pump starts; on its own it runs {{ex.4.out.appliance_count|int}} inverter ACs of 1.5 ton. Above this size most homes should look at three-phase sets and a changeover switch fitted by a licensed electrician.

mistakes: Reading kVA as kW. A {{out.kva|1}} kVA set gives {{out.capacity_w|int}} W, not {{out.kva|1}} kW; the power factor takes the rest.

Checking running watts only. A non-inverter AC, fridge or water pump draws several times its running watts for a second or two at start (the appliance data on this site uses three to six times), and that moment is what trips the generator.

Loading the generator to its full rating for hours. Keep the steady load near {{out.max_running_w|int}} W on a {{out.kva|1}} kVA set, not {{out.capacity_w|int}} W, or the engine overheats and the voltage drops.
Starting everything at once after an outage. Switch the AC on first, let it settle, then the fridge and pump; two motors starting together add their surges.
safety: Never plug a generator into a wall socket (back-feeding can electrocute line workers and burn the house wiring). Use a proper changeover switch fitted by a licensed electrician, run the set outdoors away from windows because of carbon monoxide, and earth it as the manual says.

faq.q: Can a 5 kVA generator run a 1.5 ton AC?
faq.a: An inverter AC, yes: {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.running_w|int}} W running and {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.starting_w|int}} W at most, inside the {{out.capacity_w|int}} W of a {{out.kva|1}} kVA set, with room for fans, lights and a fridge. A non-inverter AC, no by the sizing rule: its compressor start of about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W exceeds the capacity, and it needs {{ex.3.out.kva|1}} kVA.

faq.q: Can a 3 kVA generator run a fridge?
faq.a: Yes. A non-inverter fridge runs at {{a.refrigerator-non-inverter.running_w|int}} W and starts at about {{a.refrigerator-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W, inside the {{ex.1.out.capacity_w|int}} W of a {{ex.1.out.kva|1}} kVA set. With four fans, ten bulbs and a TV the whole list runs at {{ex.1.out.running_w|int}} W and peaks at {{ex.1.out.peak_w|int}} W.

faq.q: How many ACs can a 5 kVA generator run?
faq.a: On its own, {{out.appliance_count|int}} inverter ACs of 1.5 ton ({{out.appliance_run_w|int}} W each running). Add fans, lights and a fridge and one AC is the practical limit, because the running load must stay under about {{out.max_running_w|int}} W.

faq.q: What is the 5 kVA generator load capacity in watts?
faq.a: {{out.capacity_w|int}} W at {{out.pf|2}} power factor. Plan on about {{out.max_running_w|int}} W of continuous load and keep any motor start under {{out.max_start_w|int}} W in total.

faq.q: Can a 2.5 kVA generator run an AC?
faq.a: A 1 ton inverter AC, yes: with two fans and six bulbs the load is {{ex.0.out.running_w|int}} W against a running limit of {{ex.0.out.max_running_w|int}} W. No non-inverter AC fits, because even a 1 ton unit starts at about {{a.ac-split-1ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W, more than the {{ex.0.out.capacity_w|int}} W capacity.

faq.q: What can a 7 kVA generator run?
faq.a: A {{ex.3.out.kva|1}} kVA set gives {{ex.3.out.capacity_w|int}} W and about {{ex.3.out.max_running_w|int}} W of steady load: one 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with fans and lights ({{ex.3.out.running_w|int}} W, peak {{ex.3.out.peak_w|int}} W). A non-inverter fridge running at the same time lifts the AC's start peak to {{ex.2.out.peak_w|int}} W, past that capacity; a {{ex.4.out.kva|1}} kVA set covers it and runs {{ex.4.out.appliance_count|int}} inverter ACs of 1.5 ton on their own.

faq.q: Why does my generator trip when the AC starts even though the watts add up?
faq.a: Because the start surge, not the running watts, is what the generator must deliver for that second. A non-inverter 1.5 ton AC needs about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-non-inverter.starting_w|int}} W to start; if that plus everything already running is above the capacity the voltage collapses and the breaker opens. Start the AC first with other loads off, or use an inverter AC.
